claims.text: An ML interatomic potential trained on a limited set of ab initio data can replace full ab initio molecular dynamics for sampling solid and liquid phases near melting.
Combining the ML potential with enhanced sampling can accurately evaluate solid–liquid free-energy differences.
The proposed approach can retain vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling.
The proposed approach can reduce total computational cost by at least an order of magnitude relative to explicit ab initio MD and TOR-TILD.
The initial validation systems will be elemental and simple binary metals near melting, such as aluminum and Al–Cu.
A modest ab initio MD training set can capture the temperature-dependent potential-energy surfaces of both solid and liquid phases.
Umbrella sampling or a similar enhanced-sampling protocol will be used with the ML potential to evaluate solid–liquid free-energy differences.
The method will be tested from approximately 0.8 Tm to 1.2 Tm.
Reproduction of phase-specific bonding and local structural motifs will mediate accurate free-energy and entropy predictions in both phases.
Once trained, the ML potential will interpolate the ab initio potential-energy surface with high fidelity.
Enhanced sampling with the ML potential will reduce the number of computationally expensive ab initio MD steps.
Sampling the ML potential will preserve the entropic and anharmonic contributions governing fusion properties.
Free-energy evaluations will agree with explicit ab initio MD to within approximately 5%.
The method will provide a speedup of approximately 10–100 times relative to TOR-TILD for elemental and binary systems.
The expected validity boundary is elemental and binary alloys near their melting temperatures.
Transferability to multicomponent high-entropy alloys and full treatment of electron–vibration coupling remain uncertain.
Deviation exceeding 5% in solid–liquid free-energy differences relative to explicit ab initio MD will falsify the hypothesis.
Deviation exceeding 5–10% in melting temperature or latent heat relative to explicit ab initio MD will falsify the hypothesis.
